claim: A functional benefit of attention is to proactively enhance perceptual sensitivity in space and time.
source: A functional benefit of attention is to proactively enhance perceptual sensitivity in space and time.
evidence: This is a general statement about attention function presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study, but draws on established scientific understanding.

claim: Attentional orienting has traditionally been associated with cortico-thalamic networks.
source: Although attentional orienting has traditionally been associated with cortico-thalamic networks
evidence: This statement references established scientific consensus about the neural basis of attention.

claim: Individuals with cerebellar degeneration show a reduced reaction time benefit from cues that enable temporal anticipation.
source: recent evidence has shown that individuals with cerebellar degeneration (CD) show a reduced reaction time benefit from cues that enable temporal anticipation.
evidence: This refers to previous research findings, implicitly citing prior work by the authors.

claim: The CD group showed no duration-specific perceptual sensitivity benefit when cued by repeated but aperiodic presentation of the target interval.
source: Strikingly, the CD group showed no duration-specific perceptual sensitivity benefit when cued by repeated but aperiodic presentation of the target interval.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: CD participants performed similar to controls when cued by a rhythmic stream.
source: In contrast, they performed similar to controls when cued by a rhythmic stream.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data comparing CD and control groups.

claim: The cerebellum has a role in the attentional adjustment of perceptual sensitivity in time in addition to its well-documented role in motor timing.
source: This dissociation further specifies the functional domain of the cerebellum and establishes its role in the attentional adjustment of perceptual sensitivity in time in addition to its well-documented role in motor timing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and integrates with established knowledge about cerebellar motor function.

claim: The brain is anticipatory in time.
source: While the majority of research on the underlying mechanisms has focused on spatial orienting, the brain is also anticipatory in time (Nobre and van Ede, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The brain exploits various temporal regularities in the environment to predict the timing of upcoming sensory events.
source: In temporal anticipation, the brain exploits various temporal regularities in the environment to predict the timing of upcoming sensory events.
evidence: This describes a general mechanism of temporal anticipation based on established understanding.

claim: Temporal expectations can guide temporal orienting to increase perceptual sensitivity at expected compared to unexpected times.
source: These temporal expectations can guide temporal orienting, the adjustment of attention in time to modulate perceptual sensitivity, for example, increasing it at expected compared to unexpected times (Correa et al., 2005; Rohenkohl et al., 2012; Davranche et al., 2011; Denison et al., 2017; Samaha et al., 2015; Fernández et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Temporal attention has been often associated with left inferior parietal and ventral premotor cortices.
source: This form of anticipation has been often associated with left inferior parietal and ventral premotor cortices (Davranche et al., 2011; Coull and Nobre, 1998; Bolger et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: The network involved in temporal attention overlaps with frontal-parietal components of the cortico-thalamic network traditionally implicated in attentional orienting in space.
source: a network that overlaps with frontal-parietal components of the cortico-thalamic network traditionally implicated in attentional orienting in space (Posner and Petersen, 1990; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on attention networks.

claim: Individuals with cerebellar degeneration fail to exhibit reaction time benefits from temporal cues on a simple detection task.
source: Recently, we reported that individuals with cerebellar degeneration (CD) fail to exhibit reaction time benefits from temporal cues on a simple detection task (Breska and Ivry, 2018; Breska and Ivry, 2020).
evidence: This refers to previous findings by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: The findings implicate the cerebellum in temporal preparation.
source: These findings implicate the cerebellum in temporal preparation
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited previous findings.

claim: The previous findings do not enable determination of whether the cerebellum has a role in attentional modulation of perceptual systems, in motor preparation, or in both.
source: but do not enable to determine whether it has a role in attentional modulation of perceptual systems, in motor preparation, or in both.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of previous experimental designs.

claim: In speeded detection tasks, reaction time benefits from temporal cues could result from adjustment of perceptual sensitivity and/or of motor preparation.
source: This is because in speeded detection tasks, reaction time benefits from temporal cues could result from adjustment of perceptual sensitivity and/or of motor preparation (Rohenkohl et al., 2012; Sanabria et al., 2011; Morillon et al., 2016; van Ede et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the interpretation of speeded detection tasks.

claim: The cerebellum has a well-documented role in precisely timed movement.
source: Given the well-documented role of the cerebellum in precisely timed movement (Ivry and Keele, 1989; Perrett et al., 1993)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established research on cerebellar motor function.

claim: The impairments observed in the CD group may merely reflect a novel manifestation of the cerebellar role in the temporal control of motor preparation.
source: the impairments we observed in the CD group may merely reflect a novel manifestation of the cerebellar role in the temporal control of motor preparation (Shalev et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The cerebellum could be essential to attentional orienting in time to proactively modulate perception.
source: However, in addition to its role in motor timing, the cerebellum could also be essential to attentional orienting in time to proactively modulate perception.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis that the study aims to test.

claim: Determining the functional domain of the cerebellum in temporal anticipation is critical to both models of attention and of cerebellar function.
source: Determining the functional domain of the cerebellum in temporal anticipation is critical to both models of attention and of cerebellar function.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical importance of the research question.

claim: In a challenging non-speeded perceptual discrimination task, the benefits of attention are assumed to reflect modulation of perceptual sensitivity.
source: To address this question, we compared the ability of individuals with CD and healthy controls to use temporal cues to benefit performance in a challenging non-speeded perceptual discrimination task, in which the benefits of attention are assumed to reflect modulation of perceptual sensitivity (Correa et al., 2005; Davranche et al., 2011; Raymond et al., 1992).
evidence: This methodological assumption is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Participants judged the orientation of a briefly presented visual target whose contrast was set to be near-threshold.
source: Participants judged the orientation of a briefly presented visual target whose contrast was set to be near-threshold, making the task perceptually demanding.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: In each trial, a temporal cue indicated that the interval between the target and a preceding warning signal would either be 600 or 1000 ms.
source: In each trial, a temporal cue indicated that the interval between the target and a preceding warning signal (WS) would either be 600 or 1000 ms (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and references Figure 1A.

claim: Targets mostly appeared at the cued time (valid trials) and rarely at the uncued time (invalid trials).
source: Targets mostly appeared at the cued time (valid trials) and rarely at the uncued time (invalid trials).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation of cue validity.

claim: Participants were only queried for a response after a substantial random delay following target offset.
source: Critically, participants were only queried for a response after a substantial random delay following target offset.
evidence: This describes a key methodological feature of the experimental design.

claim: The inclusion of the delay eliminated the need for motor preparation.
source: In tandem with our instructions that only emphasized accuracy, the inclusion of the delay eliminated the need for motor preparation.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the methodological manipulation.

claim: The expected performance advantage on valid compared to invalid trials will reflect temporally focused enhancement of perceptual sensitivity.
source: With these manipulations, we assume that the expected performance advantage on valid compared to invalid trials (validity effect; Correa et al., 2005; Coull and Nobre, 1998; Miniussi et al., 1999; Rohenkohl et al., 2014; Breska and Deouell, 2017) will reflect temporally focused enhancement of perceptual sensitivity.
evidence: This is an assumption about the interpretation of the validity effect, supported by citations.

claim: If the cerebellum has a causal role in attention orienting in time at a non-motor level, the validity effect should be reduced in CD patients relative to controls.
source: If the cerebellum has a causal role in attention orienting in time at a non-motor level, the validity effect should be reduced in CD patients relative to controls.
evidence: This is a testable prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: In previous work, cerebellar involvement was limited to when temporal anticipation required encoding and recalling an isolated interval, but not when temporal anticipation could be based on synchronization with a stream of rhythmic sensory events.
source: In our previous work (Breska and Ivry, 2018; Breska and Ivry, 2020), we found that the cerebellar involvement was limited to when temporal anticipation required encoding and recalling an isolated interval, but not when temporal anticipation could be based on synchronization with a stream of rhythmic sensory events.
evidence: This refers to findings from previous studies by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: The study compared perceptual benefits from interval and rhythmic temporal cues.
source: We employ a similar manipulation in the present study, comparing perceptual benefits from interval and rhythmic temporal cues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and references Figure 1B.

claim: In two-interval designs, the validity effect is less robust or even absent for late targets.
source: Prior work has shown that in two-interval designs as implemented here, the validity effect is less robust or even absent for late targets (van Ede et al., 2020; Miniussi et al., 1999; Correa et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neither group showed a significant validity effect in either task for the late onset targets.
source: Indeed, neither group showed a significant validity effect in either task for the late onset targets (all uncorrected p's > 0.09, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis, referencing a supplementary figure.

claim: The control group showed a higher mean d' for valid compared to invalid trials in the interval task.
source: The control group showed a higher mean d' for valid compared to invalid trials (t(11)=3.08, p=0.011, Cohen's d=0.89)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: In the interval task, d' values in the CD group were not significantly different between valid and invalid trials, and even numerically higher on invalid trials.
source: while d' values in the CD group were not significantly different, and even numerically higher on invalid trials (t(12) = −0.43, p=0.67, BF10=0.21, moderate evidence against a directional hypothesis of a validity effect).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis, including Bayesian analysis.

claim: The CD group failed to show an enhancement in perceptual sensitivity from an interval-based temporal cue.
source: Thus, the CD group failed to show an enhancement in perceptual sensitivity from an interval-based temporal cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical results.

claim: The control group showed a validity effect in the rhythm task.
source: The control group again showed a validity effect (t(11)=2.67, p=0.022, Cohen's d=0.77).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The CD group showed a validity effect in the rhythm task.
source: However, unlike in the interval task, the CD group also showed a validity effect (t(12)=3.45, p=0.005, Cohen's d=0.95).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The ability to increase perceptual sensitivity at a specific time point based on a rhythm cue was preserved in the CD group.
source: Thus, the ability to increase perceptual sensitivity at a specific time point based on a rhythm cue was preserved in the CD group.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical results.

claim: The attenuation of the validity effect in the CD group relative to controls was significantly larger in the interval task than in the rhythm task.
source: Furthermore, the presence of the three-way interaction implies that the attenuation of the validity effect in the CD group relative to controls was significantly larger in the interval task than in the rhythm task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical interaction effect.

claim: The results provide compelling evidence that the integrity of the human cerebellum is necessary for proactive modulation of perceptual processing based on temporal expectations.
source: Our results provide compelling evidence that the integrity of the human cerebellum is necessary for proactive modulation of perceptual processing based on temporal expectations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The ability to use a temporal cue to enhance perceptual sensitivity at specific times was abolished in individuals with CD when prediction was based on an interval cue.
source: The ability to use a temporal cue to enhance perceptual sensitivity at specific times was abolished in individuals with CD when prediction was based on an interval cue.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The CD group showed a comparable benefit to controls when temporal orienting was based on a rhythmic cue.
source: In contrast, the CD group showed a comparable benefit to controls when temporal orienting was based on a rhythmic cue.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The use of a non-speeded, challenging perceptual discrimination task argues strongly against the idea that the impairment is related to motor preparation processes.
source: Critically, the use of a non-speeded, challenging perceptual discrimination task argues strongly against the idea that the impairment is related to motor preparation processes.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the findings based on the experimental design.

claim: The results point to an essential context-specific role of the cerebellum in the temporal orienting of visual attention.
source: Rather, the results point to an essential context-specific role of the cerebellum in the temporal orienting of visual attention
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The cerebellum is involved in a broad range of cognitive functions beyond the motor domain.
source: adding to the substantial literature highlighting cerebellar involvement in a broad range of cognitive functions beyond the motor domain (Sokolov et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review of the literature.

claim: The findings point to the need for an expanded picture of the neuroanatomical network involved in attentional control of perceptual sensitivity.
source: These findings point to the need for an expanded picture of the neuroanatomical network involved in attentional control of perceptual sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference about the theoretical implications of the findings.

claim: Attention research has traditionally emphasized cortico-thalamic networks, particularly dorsal and ventral fronto-parietal networks associated with top-down and stimulus-driven attention control.
source: Attention research has traditionally emphasized cortico-thalamic networks, and in particular, dorsal and ventral fronto-parietal networks associated with top-down and stimulus-driven attention control, respectively (Posner and Petersen, 1990; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational work on attention networks.

claim: Human imaging studies consistently reveal activations of the left inferior parietal cortex and the ventral premotor cortex for attention orienting in the time domain.
source: For attention orienting in the time domain, human imaging studies consistently reveal activations of the left inferior parietal cortex and the ventral premotor cortex (Davranche et al., 2011; Coull and Nobre, 1998; Bolger et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Neural signatures of temporal anticipation identified in human electrophysiology studies have been localized to cortico-thalamic circuits.
source: Similarly, neural signatures of temporal anticipation identified in human electrophysiology studies have been localized to cortico-thalamic circuits (Gómez et al., 2001; Praamstra, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: The cerebellum has not featured in attention research, perhaps due to the difficulty in neuroimaging studies to separate the effects of temporal prediction on neural activations from the effects of other task parameters, or the difficulty of electrophysiology studies to measure cerebellar sources.
source: In general, the cerebellum has not featured in this work, perhaps due to the difficulty in neuroimaging studies to separate the effects of temporal prediction on neural activations from the effects of other task parameters, or the difficulty of electrophysiology studies to measure cerebellar sources.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of cerebellar findings in prior attention research.

claim: O'Reilly et al., 2008 observed greater cerebellar activation for detecting violations of spatio-temporal predictions compared to spatial predictions, pointing to cerebellar involvement in temporal prediction.
source: One exception here is a study by O'Reilly et al., 2008 who observed greater cerebellar activation for detecting violations of spatio-temporal predictions compared to spatial predictions, pointing to cerebellar involvement in temporal prediction (O'Reilly et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific neuroimaging study.

claim: The current findings demonstrate that the cerebellum has a causal role in temporal anticipation.
source: The current findings demonstrate that the cerebellum has a causal role in temporal anticipation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The current findings establish the cerebellum's role in using temporal information to modulate attention for the perceptual analysis of visual features.
source: and establish its role in using temporal information to modulate attention for the perceptual analysis of visual features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The neuropsychological approach provides a more direct method to evaluate the contribution of the cerebellum to attention.
source: Our neuropsychological approach provides a more direct method to evaluate the contribution of the cerebellum to attention.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological advantage of the study design.

claim: Previous work on spatial attention has proven inconclusive regarding cerebellar involvement.
source: Previous work, focusing on the spatial domain, has proven inconclusive.
evidence: This is a summary statement about prior research.

claim: Some studies have found that individuals with focal cerebellar lesions show reduced benefits from cues indicating the spatial location of a forthcoming stimulus.
source: Some studies have found that individuals with focal cerebellar lesions show reduced benefits from cues indicating the spatial location of a forthcoming stimulus (Townsend et al., 1999; Allen et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: It has been proposed that spatial attention impairments in cerebellar patients may be motoric in nature, with the tasks confounding attentional demands with demands on eye movements and/or response preparation.
source: However, it has been proposed that these impairments may be motoric in nature, with the tasks confounding attentional demands with demands on eye movements and/or response preparation (Ravizza and Ivry, 2001; Haarmeier and Thier, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to critical analyses of prior studies.

claim: The concerns about motor confounds in spatial attention studies do not apply to the current study given that the spatial aspects of the task were fixed and the motor requirements were minimal, delayed until well after stimulus offset.
source: These concerns do not apply to the current study given that the spatial aspects of the task were fixed and the motor requirements were minimal, delayed until well after stimulus offset.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological advantages of the current study design.

claim: The current results do not address the question of whether the cerebellum, in addition to its role in temporal orienting of attention, is also involved in other spheres of attention.
source: We note that the current results do not address the question of whether the cerebellum, in addition to its role in temporal orienting of attention, is also involved in other spheres of attention.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study's scope.

claim: A longstanding debate in the timing literature concerns whether temporal anticipation in a rhythmic context is mediated by rhythm-specific mechanisms (e.g., entrainment) or by the repeated operation of an interval-based mechanism.
source: First, a longstanding debate in the timing literature concerns whether temporal anticipation in a rhythmic context is mediated by rhythm-specific mechanisms (e.g., entrainment) or by the repeated operation of an interval-based mechanism (Breska and Deouell, 2017; Haegens and Zion Golumbic, 2018; Drake and Botte, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The results are at odds with the hypothesis that rhythmic temporal anticipation is mediated by the repeated operation of an interval-based mechanism.
source: Our results are at odds with the latter hypothesis given that the CD group failed to benefit from the interval cues yet showed normal benefits from the rhythm cues.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dissociation observed in the experimental findings.

claim: Beat-based timing may rely on cortico-striatal circuits even in the absence of movement.
source: Beat-based timing may rely on cortico-striatal circuits even in the absence of movement (Cannon and Patel, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Previous findings showed impaired rhythm-based temporal prediction in Parkinson's disease.
source: consistent with previous findings of impaired rhythm-based temporal prediction in Parkinson's disease (Breska and Ivry, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The selective contribution of the cerebellum in interval-based but not rhythm-based contexts has been observed in multiple timing domains, including duration judgments, timed movement, and timed motor preparation.
source: Second, the selective contribution of the cerebellum in interval-based but not rhythm-based contexts has been observed in multiple timing domains, including duration judgments, timed movement, and timed motor preparation (Breska and Ivry, 2018; Breska and Ivry, 2020; Grube et al., 2010; Spencer et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research across multiple domains.

claim: The findings extend the functional specificity of cerebellar involvement to the attentional domain, pointing to a generalized role for the cerebellum in interval timing, at least in the sub-second range.
source: Our findings extend this functional specificity to the attentional domain, pointing to a generalized role for the cerebellum in interval timing, at in the sub-second range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the context of prior research.

claim: An intuitive hypothesis is that the cerebellum is necessary for the temporal processing of isolated intervals.
source: Given the cerebellar involvement in interval-based timing across timing domains, an intuitive hypothesis is that the cerebellum is necessary for the temporal processing of isolated intervals (Ivry and Keele, 1989; Ivry and Schlerf, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The cerebellar role in interval timing could reflect a central role in the formation of a temporal representation or retrieval processes related to interval memory.
source: This could reflect a central role in one or both of two putative functional subcomponents in interval timing models (Addyman et al., 2016; Gibbon et al., 1984), the formation of a temporal representation or retrieval processes related to interval memory.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the computational role of the cerebellum, supported by citations to timing models.

claim: Predictive processing in non-cerebellar circuits may rely on cerebellar interval timing capacities to parameterize the temporal dimension of the prediction.
source: By this view, predictive processing in non-cerebellar circuits (e.g., prefrontal cortex) relies on cerebellar interval timing capacities to parameterize the temporal dimension of the prediction.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional relationship between cerebellar and cortical circuits.

claim: In rhythm-based orienting, an interval-based mechanism would not be required as the temporal parameters are contained within ongoing neural dynamics.
source: In rhythm-based orienting, an interval-based mechanism would not be required as the temporal parameters are contained within ongoing neural dynamics.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the dissociation observed in the findings.

claim: A broader hypothesis is that the interval-based prediction itself is formed within the cerebellum, part of the cerebellar role in prediction in the motor domain and beyond.
source: However, a broader hypothesis is that the interval-based prediction itself is formed within the cerebellum, part of the cerebellar role in prediction in the motor domain and beyond (Sokolov et al., 2017; Wolpert et al., 1998; Miall et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to prior theoretical work on cerebellar prediction.

claim: Cerebellar temporal predictions may guide proactive modulation in non-cerebellar circuits according to task goals.
source: By this view, these cerebellar temporal predictions guide proactive modulation in non-cerebellar circuits according to task goals (e.g., to prepare perceptual or motor systems).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional role of cerebellar predictions.

claim: In rhythm-based orienting, dedicated prediction mechanisms are not necessary due to the self-sustaining limit cycle properties of the putatively entrained oscillatory dynamics.
source: In rhythm-based orienting, dedicated prediction mechanisms are not necessary due to the self-sustaining limit cycle properties of the putatively entrained oscillatory dynamics.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on theoretical models of neural oscillations.

claim: Future work should aim to explore the separability of timing and prediction, identifying the cerebellar computations that provide the essential information for temporal orienting.
source: Future work should aim to explore the separability of timing and prediction, identifying the cerebellar computations that provide the essential information for temporal orienting.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Fifteen individuals with CD and 14 age-matched neurotypical control individuals were recruited for the study.
source: Fifteen individuals with CD and 14 age-matched neurotypical control individuals were recruited for the study.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the study.

claim: The final sample size was 13 CD and 12 control participants after exclusions.
source: Thus, the final sample size was 13 CD and 12 control participants.
evidence: This describes the final sample after exclusions.

claim: The sample size was determined using power calculations to allow 80% power to detect effects with Cohen's d = 0.8.
source: The sample size was determined using power calculations to allow 80% power to detect effects with Cohen's d = 0.8 (a conservative estimate, given the typical effect size of temporal cuing in prior studies: Cohen's d = 1–1.5; Rohenkohl et al., 2012; Breska and Ivry, 2018; Rohenkohl et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the sample size, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of California, Berkeley.
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of California, Berkeley.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants in the CD group had been diagnosed with spinocerebellar ataxia, a slowly progressive adult-onset degenerative disorder in which the primary pathology involves atrophy of the cerebellum.
source: Participants in the CD group (9 females, 12 right-handed, mean age = 56.2 years, SD = 11.1) had been diagnosed with spinocerebellar ataxia, a slowly progressive adult-onset degenerative disorder in which the primary pathology involves atrophy of the cerebellum.
evidence: This describes the clinical characteristics of the CD group.

claim: The CD and control groups did not differ significantly in age.
source: The CD and control groups did not differ significantly in age (p=0.52).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing the groups.

claim: There was no significant group difference in MoCA scores between CD and control groups.
source: Although we did not select participants to provide a match on this measure, there was no significant group difference (CD: mean = 26.7, control: mean = 27.5, p=0.32).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing cognitive assessment scores.

claim: The mean contrast level did not differ between groups.
source: Consistent with our expectation, the mean contrast level did not differ between groups (t(23)=0.83, p=0.41).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing the perceptual threshold between groups.

claim: Perceptual sensitivity was quantified using d', a measure derived from signal detection theory.
source: Perceptual sensitivity was quantified using d', a measure derived from signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: This describes the analysis method, supported by a citation to the foundational work on signal detection theory.

claim: Temporal orienting should manifest as higher d' for valid compared to invalid trials.
source: Temporal orienting should manifest as higher d' for valid compared to invalid trials.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on signal detection theory.
